# Distributed Team Effectiveness Initiative
## Communication, Collaboration and Conflict in Geographically Dispersed Project Teams — Recommendation for Sponsor Group

**Version 1.0 — first circulation. Prepared for sponsor group discussion, and for prior circulation to the delivery leads of the eleven affected programmes and to the four regional engineering directors. Not yet for team-wide communication.**

---

### How we would ask you to use this

One note, then the substance.

This paper takes the brief at its word and then, respectfully, tests it. The brief describes *communication delays and occasional misunderstandings*. That may be exactly what we have. It may also be what a dependency-architecture problem looks like from the outside, in which case communication training will make the symptom articulate without making it smaller. §2 sets out how we would tell the difference, cheaply, before anyone commits to a design.

The team cards in §9 are **working hypotheses, offered so they can be corrected**. A card returned unamended will be read not as agreement but as a sign that the conversation has not happened, and we would come back for it. Where a team has its own instrumented data, that data supersedes the card and the card is retired (§9.1).

Two courtesies we would ask before this travels further. First, that the delivery leads see §§3, 4 and 11 and have time to respond in their own register before the board pack closes — a paper about distributed authority that arrives in a team fully formed has already lost its argument, and people will notice that before they notice anything else. Second, that §12 (monitoring, consultation and data gates) be walked through with Group Legal, the Data Protection Officer and the European Works Council secretariat **before any measurement is switched on**. Most of what we propose to measure in §10 is, in several jurisdictions, employee monitoring. That is a co-determination and lawful-basis question, not a dashboard question, and getting it in the wrong order is the single most likely source of avoidable damage here.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Reduce the need for synchronous coordination rather than increasing its supply; fix a thin global core of five team entitlements stated as floors; devolve all norms, rituals, tooling choices and cadence to the teams themselves via a charter they write; run four instrumented pilots with deliberately different designs and identical measurement; and bind the centre and the co-located majority to the same discipline asked of everyone else.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Core insight | The constraint is rarely goodwill or skill. It is **dependency density across time-zone boundaries**, compounded by asymmetric access to informal context |
| Global mandate | **Five entitlements only** (§3) — a named owner for every cross-site dependency; a maximum time-to-first-substantive-response; a discoverable written record of every decision; a route to contribute in writing and, where needed, in one's own language; a stated fallback when work meets a sleeping time zone. Each a floor, each with an alternative-form route (§3.7) |
| Devolved to teams | Channels, tools, ceremony, meeting cadence, standup format, working hours, escalation style, documentation depth, and the team's own vocabulary. Written by the team into a charter (§7) the team owns |
| Structural move | **Time-zone-native ownership** of whole decision classes rather than split ownership across zones (§5.3). This is the intervention we expect to matter most and it is not a communication intervention at all |
| Fairness rule | Out-of-hours meeting burden is **measured, published and rotated**. The co-located majority takes its share (§5.5, §11.2) |
| The centre's obligation | **Corridor decisions are void** until written (§11.1). Reversals of team-level decisions require written reasons to the same audience that saw the decision, counted and reported quarterly |
| Conflict doctrine | Four species distinguished (§8); latency assumed before intent; blameless misunderstanding review; a **bridge role that is earned, rotating and explicitly not managerial** (§8.4) |
| Measurement | Behavioural proxies weighted 70%, survey items 30%; response-style correction applied before any cross-site comparison is shown (§10.2) |
| Numeric failure test | Survey "communication effectiveness" index +5 points or more while median time-to-first-substantive-response on cross-site requests improves <15% and blocked-work hours are flat = **declared failure, programme paused, no further capital** (§10.4) |
| Investment sought | **$3.9M Year 1, $2.6M Year 2** (illustrative, assumptions at §14.1), of which **$1.7M is protected documentation and handover time** — the line most often cut and most often fatal |
| Funding split | Central funds diagnostic, instrumentation, tooling, facilitation; programmes fund protected time with a **60% central offset in Y1, 30% in Y2, nil thereafter** (§14.2) |
| Decisions requested | **Three** — §14.4, sought at the sponsor group meeting on **22 April** |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

*Distributed teams do not fail because people are far apart. They fail because work is arranged as though they were not.*

This is our considered practitioner assertion, not a finding — see the evidence key at §15. We flag it because the sponsor group is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are judgement.

The specific failure we are trying to avoid is familiar: a communication programme is launched, a set of norms is published, everyone becomes fluent in the vocabulary of "over-communication" and "assume positive intent," and nothing measurable moves except the survey. That outcome is worse than no initiative, because it consumes the credibility a second attempt would need.

---

## 2. Diagnosis before design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the sponsor group to test

Six candidate drivers produce the same reported symptom. Only two of them respond to communication practice work; two are made *worse* by it.

| Candidate driver | What communication training does to it |
|---|---|
| Too many cross-zone dependencies per unit of work | Nothing — requires work decomposition and ownership redesign (§5) |
| Decision rights held at a site that does not hold the information | **Amplifies harm** — faster, more confident, still wrong |
| Informal context accrues only to the co-located subgroup | Nothing until corridor decisions are made visible and costly (§11.1) |
| No shared written record; decisions live in memory and DMs | Improves, *if* paired with funded documentation time (§3.4) |
| Working-language asymmetry suppresses contribution | Nothing — needs channel design and drafting time, not confidence-building (§6.4) |
| Genuine norm divergence on directness, deadlines, escalation | **Improves** — this is the part the initiative is actually good at (§4) |
| Unanswered questions carry no consequence for anyone | **Worsens** — a further unanswered invitation deepens cynicism |

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Five weeks. No design freeze until it reports.

| Component | Detail |
|---|---|
| Dependency map | For six representative project teams: every cross-site dependency, its owner, its median wait. This is the single most informative artefact and we have never once found it already to exist |
| Latency instrumentation | Retrospective pull from existing ticketing and repository systems: time-to-first-substantive-response, by site pair, by direction. **Aggregate only; §12** |
| Silence audit | Threads and requests that received no substantive response at all within 10 working days. Counted, not attributed |
| Structured conversations | 48 conversations across four levels in seven countries, including at least two teams whose members have never met |
| Meeting burden ledger | Out-of-hours synchronous hours per person per site, from calendar metadata, aggregated by site |
| Language check | The four teams whose working language is not the local language of the majority of members |
| Cost | **$185K** |

**The decision this buys.** If the dependency map shows high cross-zone dependency density, the Year 1 budget should move substantially from practice-and-behaviour work into work decomposition and ownership redesign, and the pilot scope should be rewritten before commitment. This is the cheapest consequential decision available to us, and we would rather make it in May than discover it in November.

---

## 3. What is fixed everywhere: five entitlements, stated as floors

Framed as what a team member is *entitled to*, not as how anyone must behave — so that very different conduct can honour the same floor.

### 3.1 Entitlement I — every cross-site dependency has a named owner
**Floor:** any member can name, for each thing their work waits on, a single named person and the decision that is awaited. Not a team, not a distribution list, not a role — a person. Where nobody can be named, the dependency is escalated as a *design* defect, not a behavioural one.

### 3.2 Entitlement II — there is a maximum time-to-first-substantive-response, and it is visible
**Floor:** each team publishes latency classes and holds to them.

| Class | Response commitment (default, teams may set their own) |
|---|---|
| Blocking — work stopped | One working day of the recipient, with a named fallback if unavailable |
| Consequential, not blocking | Two working days |
| Everything else | Best effort, explicitly no commitment |

*"I have read this, I cannot answer until Thursday, here is who can"* satisfies the floor. Silence does not. **The floor is the acknowledgement, not the answer** — this distinction is the whole of it, and teams that miss it produce anxiety rather than speed.

### 3.3 Entitlement III — decisions are discoverable in writing
**Floor:** any decision that changes what someone else must do exists, within 24 hours, in a location a new joiner could find unaided. Format devolved entirely — a paragraph in a channel is sufficient. Length is not the point; findability is.

### 3.4 Entitlement IV — there is a written route in, and language is not a tax on contribution
**Floor:** every member has at least one channel through which they may contribute, and disagree, **in writing and asynchronously**, and receive a response. It need never be a spoken objection on a live call in a second language.

Where a member's working-language fluency is materially below the team median, they are entitled to draft in their own language with machine translation, and to have that carry the same weight. This is a floor because the alternative — treating fluency as a proxy for contribution — is both unjust and expensively wrong.

### 3.5 Entitlement V — no work sleeps without a stated fallback
**Floor:** for each work item crossing a time-zone boundary, either a named person in the receiving zone can progress it, or the handover states explicitly that it will wait and until when. **The prohibited state is not delay. It is undeclared delay.**

### 3.6 Everything else is the team's property
Tools, cadence, standups, ceremony, documentation depth, escalation style, core hours, camera norms, emoji conventions, and the team's own name for all of this. We would suggest the centre resist standardising even the vocabulary.

### 3.7 The alternative-form process (in place of exemption)

We avoid the word *exemption*, and avoid asking any team to refuse. A team that cannot meet a floor is asked instead to **propose the nearest form it can honour**, and to state the condition under which the floor becomes reachable.

| Element | Provision |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Legal impossibility, collective-agreement conflict, client-contractual conflict, or structural impossibility — not difficulty, not preference |
| Form | Two pages: which floor, why, the alternative mechanism, the condition that would close the gap |
| Approver | Programme director, countersigned by the regional engineering director and, where data or monitoring is implicated, Group Legal |
| Duration | 12 months, renewable once with fresh reasoning |
| Visibility | Internally published register, reviewed quarterly |
| Presumption | Accepted unless materially weaker than the floor. We expect three to six across the network in Year 1 and would be suspicious of zero |

---

## 4. The adaptation logic

### 4.1 Four axes, not a culture model

We would ask each team to place *itself* — not its nationalities — on four axes, because these four determine whether a given practice functions or backfires.

| Axis | The question | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Directness of disagreement** | Can dissent be public without cost to either party? | Whether the dissent route can be a live call, or must be written and private (Entitlement IV) |
| **Context density** | Is meaning carried in the words, or in what surrounds them? | How much explicit writing is required before a message is complete |
| **Authority basis** | Does authority derive from role, or from demonstrated expertise? | Whether devolved ownership reads as trust or as abandonment |
| **Time orientation** | Is a date a commitment, a forecast, or an aspiration? | Whether "on track" means the same thing on both ends of a call |

### 4.2 The working rule

> Low disagreement-directness does not mean people have nothing to say. It means **the channel is wrong, not the culture**. An open invitation on a live call in a second language in front of a senior colleague is not an invitation; it is a test most people will sensibly decline to sit.

The functioning equivalent is almost always: written, asynchronous, addressed to a named person, with time to draft, and — where face matters — routed so that no one is corrected in public. Our practitioner judgement is that moving the dissent channel from spoken-live to written-async recovers more suppressed information than any amount of psychological-safety framing. Offered as judgement (§15), and testable inside the pilots via the silence audit.

### 4.3 The four misreadings we expect

| One side does | The other reads | The actual meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Answers "yes, we can look at that" | Commitment | Acknowledgement of the request's legitimacy |
| Sends a three-line message with no preamble | Coldness, possible anger | Efficiency, and respect for the reader's time |
| Reports "on track" until the week before | Concealment | Reluctance to escalate upward without a solution in hand |
| Goes silent for two days | Disengagement | A public holiday nobody outside that country had heard of |

The last one is not a joke. A shared holiday-and-absence calendar, visible by default, retires a meaningful share of reported "misunderstandings" for approximately no money. We would put it in the first thirty days.

---

## 5. Time-zone architecture — the part that is not about communication

### 5.1 The arithmetic, stated plainly

| Overlap between two sites | What is realistically possible |
|---|---|
| 4+ hours | Genuinely collaborative work; joint problem-solving |
| 2–3 hours | Coordination and decision-making; not sustained joint work |
| 0–1 hours | **Handover only.** Any design that assumes more will fail, and no amount of goodwill will rescue it |

### 5.2 The default we recommend

Redraw team boundaries so that each **decision loop** sits inside a zone band with ≥4 hours of overlap, and each **handover** sits at a band boundary that is documented and deliberately chosen. Cross-band dependency count becomes a tracked engineering metric with a target, in the same manner as build time.

### 5.3 Time-zone-native ownership

Where possible, give a whole decision class to the region that holds the working hours for it, rather than splitting it and coordinating. This trades some consistency for a large reduction in latency. We regard the trade as clearly worth making and would rather argue it openly than smuggle it in.

### 5.4 Three experiments we would like permission to run

The persona of this programme is exploratory by design; these are cheap, reversible and instrumented.

| Experiment | Duration | What it tests |
|---|---|---|
| **Async-only fortnight** — all recurring cross-zone meetings cancelled, nothing else changed | 2 weeks, two pilot teams | How much of our meeting load is coordination and how much is habit. We expect to be surprised in both directions |
| **Reverse-hours quarter** — the largest co-located site takes the unsociable slot for all cross-zone calls | 1 quarter, one pilot | Whether the burden is tolerable when it is reciprocal, and what the co-located site learns from carrying it |
| **Bounty board** — unblocked dependencies published openly; any qualified person in any zone may claim and resolve one | 1 quarter | Whether latency is caused by capacity or by ownership routing |

### 5.5 The fairness ledger

# Global Employee Empowerment & Adaptive Culture Initiative
## Guidance on Regional Leadership Adaptation — Recommendation for Sponsor Group

**Version 2.0 — complete. Prepared for sponsor group decision, and for prior circulation to the fourteen regional people leads. Not yet for employee communication.**

---

### How we would ask you to use this

One note only, and then the substance.

This version differs from v1.0 in three ways that the reviewers were right to insist on. It now asks for specific decisions, with money and a date attached (§12). It answers the questions the first draft deferred — most importantly what the centre itself is bound by (§9). And the regional material has been re-cut so that no colleague opens it and finds their country described inside someone else's card.

The regional cards in §6 remain what they were: **working hypotheses, offered so that they can be corrected**. Where a region has its own diagnostic data, that data replaces the card and the card is retired for that unit (§5.4). A card returned to us unamended will be read not as agreement but as a sign that the conversation has not yet taken place, and we would come back for it.

Two courtesies we would ask the sponsor group to extend before this travels further. First, that the fourteen regional people leads and the four regional MDs see §§3, 4 and 9 and have time to respond in their own way before the board pack is assembled — a programme about devolved authority that arrives in a region fully formed has already contradicted itself, and colleagues will notice that before they notice anything else. Second, that §10 (consultation and legal gates) be walked through with Group Legal, the European Works Council secretariat and Group Reward before any part of this is described to employees anywhere. The likeliest single cause of avoidable damage is a well-intentioned announcement that reaches a works council after it reaches a newspaper, or reaches an employee before it reaches their own supervisor.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Adopt a thin global core and a wide local expression: four employee entitlements defined centrally as *floors*, with a formal alternative-form process where a floor cannot lawfully or structurally be met; delivery method, language, sequencing and naming devolved entirely to regions; four instrumented pilots in Year 1 with a common measurement spine but deliberately different local design; and a published protocol binding the centre to the same discipline it asks of others.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Global mandate | **Four entitlements only** (§3) — decision rights at the lowest competent level; an answered route for dissent; tolerance of good-faith error; employee-initiated internal movement. Each stated as a floor, each with a named-approver alternative-form route (§3.6) |
| Devolved to regions | Language, ritual, sequencing, symbolism, manager incentives, pace, communication channels, and the programme's name. We would suggest the centre resist standardising even the name |
| Year 1 shape | **Four pilots — one high-authority-distance, one low, one deskless-majority, one recently-acquired entity** — different in design, identical in instrumentation (§7) |
| Principal risk | Middle-manager status and grade loss, not employee resistance (§8) |
| The centre's own obligation | **Published reversal protocol**: the centre may reverse a devolved decision, but must give written reasons to the same audience that saw the decision, and reversal counts are reported quarterly beside regional metrics (§9) |
| Measurement | Within-region trend on four behavioural proxies weighted 70%, survey items 30%; acquiescence correction applied before any cross-region view is shown (§8.3) |
| Numeric failure test | Empowerment survey index +5 points or more while decision latency on the instrumented decision class improves <10% and internal-move rate is flat = declared failure, programme paused, no further capital (§8.5) |
| Investment sought | **$14.2M Year 1, $10.6M Year 2** (illustrative, assumptions in §12.1), of which $6.9M is manager time relief — the line most often omitted and most often fatal |
| Funding split | Central P&L funds diagnostic, instrumentation, platform, central team and pilot facilitation; regions fund manager time with a **60% central offset in Y1, 30% in Y2, nil thereafter** (§12.3) |
| Decisions requested | **Three** — §12.5, sought at the sponsor group meeting on **18 March** |
| Programme owner | Group Chief People Officer, sponsor; named programme director recruited internally within 30 days of approval |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Empowerment mechanisms do not transfer between contexts; the conditions that make them work can be built in each. *(This is our considered assertion from practitioner experience, not a finding — see the evidence key at §14. We flag it because the sponsor group is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are judgement.)*

The specific failure we are trying to avoid is well documented in our own past programmes: exported behavioural vocabulary — "speak up", "own it", "disagree and commit" — produces regions that become fluent at the annual survey and unchanged on Tuesday morning. That outcome is worse than no initiative, because it consumes the credibility a second attempt would require.

---

## 2. Diagnosis before we design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the sponsor group to test

The initiative is currently described as culture change. The evidence available to us may instead describe a **decision-rights and information-flow** problem wearing culture-change clothing. Only one of those two responds to leadership behaviour work, and we would rather establish which we have before committing eight figures to the wrong one.

| Candidate driver | What leadership/empowerment training does to it |
|---|---|
| Decision rights formally held too high | Nothing — requires delegation-of-authority redesign |
| Rights delegated on paper, retracted in practice | Nothing until retraction is made visible and costly (§9) |
| Information does not reach the level holding authority | **Amplifies harm** — confident decisions on poor data |
| Managers lack coaching capability | Improves, *if* paired with funded time relief (§8.4) |
| Reward and grading pay for control, not for developing others | Nothing — the incentive wins every time (§8.2) |
| Employees have voice but no evidence it is ever acted on | Worsens — a further unanswered invitation deepens cynicism |
| Working-language barrier suppresses contribution | Nothing — needs channel design, not confidence-building (§11.1) |

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Five weeks, no design freeze until it reports: 60 structured conversations across four organisational levels in eight countries (including two deskless-majority sites); an audit of the documented delegation-of-authority matrix against actual practice in twelve units; and a language-barrier check in the four sites where the working language is not the local one. Cost **$310K**.

If it finds that decision rights are formally too high, the largest part of the Year 2 training envelope should be redirected to delegation architecture and the pilot scope revised before commitment. This is the cheapest consequential decision in the programme.

### 2.3 The uncomfortable question, now answered rather than deferred

Will headquarters be bound by the same four entitlements? If regional colleagues discover that the centre reserves the right to overturn devolved decisions without giving reasons, the initiative becomes rhetoric and everything downstream of it is wasted. v1.0 left this open. **§9 now answers it with a specific, testable, reportable mechanism**, and we would ask the sponsor group to adopt or amend it rather than to note it.

---

## 3. What is fixed everywhere: four entitlements, stated as floors

Framed as what an employee is entitled to, not as how a manager must behave, so that very different conduct can honour them.

### 3.1 Entitlement I — decision rights sit at the lowest competent level
**Floor:** every employee can name the classes of decision they own and point to a recent instance of exercising one without seeking permission. *Competent* is doing real work in that sentence; this is not an argument for uniform flat structures.

### 3.2 Entitlement II — there is a route for dissent, and it is answered
**Floor:** every employee has at least one available channel through which they can contradict a superior's view **and receive a response**. The channel may be a written pre-read, a skip-level, a facilitated small group, a mentor, a shift huddle, or an anonymous board. It need never be a raised hand in a large meeting. The answered part is the floor; the form is entirely local.

**Firewall, mandatory:** this channel is expressly **not** a statutory reporting channel. Disagreement about a business decision is not a protected disclosure. The two must be separately named, separately routed and separately governed, or we create legal exposure on one side and chill genuine reporting on the other (§10.3).

### 3.3 Entitlement III — good-faith error is absorbed, not attributed
**Floor:** within each unit, at least one specific, visible instance per quarter in which a good-faith mistake was absorbed rather than attributed, and the team can name it. Demonstrated, never announced. In several regions this must be framed collectively rather than individually to be usable at all (§6).

### 3.4 Entitlement IV — employees can initiate their own movement
**Floor (revised from v1.0):** an employee may apply for an internal role, project or rotation **without the incumbent manager holding a veto and without the manager being informed in advance of the application**.

v1.0 stated this as an absolute and was wrong to. In parts of the Gulf, mobility between entities is constrained by employer-tied work permits and is a legal matter, not a cultural one. In Japan, Korea and Taiwan, seniority-anchored career and reward structures make unrestricted lateral self-nomination structurally disruptive in ways that a global mandate cannot responsibly overrule from a distance. The floor above is the most we can hold everywhere; where even that cannot be met, §3.6 applies.

### 3.5 Everything else is regional property
Language, ceremony, sequencing, symbolism, tooling, incentives, cadence, and the programme's own name.

### 3.6 The alternative-form process (in place of exemption)

We deliberately avoid the word *exemption*, and avoid asking any region to refuse. A region that cannot meet a floor is asked instead to **propose the nearest form it can honour**, and to say what it would take to close the remainder.

| Element | Provision |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Legal impossibility, collective-agreement conflict, or structural impossibility (not difficulty, not discomfort) |
| Form | Two pages: which floor, why, the alternative mechanism proposed, and the condition under which the floor becomes reachable |
| Approver | **Group Chief People Officer**, countersigned by the Regional MD and by Group Legal |
| Duration | **12 months maximum**, renewable once with fresh reasoning |
| Visibility | Entered in an internally published register, reviewed quarterly by the sponsor group |
| Presumption | An alternative form is accepted unless it is materially weaker than the floor. We expect four to eight across the network in Year 1 and would be suspicious of zero |

---

## 4. The adaptation logic

### 4.1 Four variables, rather than a general culture model

We would ask each region to place itself on four axes only, because these four determine whether a given mechanism functions or backfires.

| Axis | The question | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Authority basis** | Does a manager's authority derive from role or from demonstrated expertise? | Whether devolution reads as trust or as abandonment |
| **Directness of disagreement** | Can dissent be public without cost to either party? | The design of the dissent channel (Entitlement II) |
| **Attribution of error** | Does a mistake attach to a person, a team, or a system? | Whether error tolerance can be individual or must be collective (III) |
| **Ambiguity tolerance** | Is an open brief experienced as freedom, or as information withheld? | How much structure must accompany autonomy |

### 4.2 The working rule

> High authority distance and low disagreement-directness do not mean empowerment is unwelcome. They mean it must be **granted rather than seized** — granted visibly, specifically, bounded, and by someone whose authority the team already accepts.

In such contexts an open invitation ("bring me your ideas") is not empowerment; it is a test most colleagues will decline to sit. The functioning equivalent is a named, bounded, publicly conferred mandate: *"Priya decides this class of exception up to this threshold. She does not need to ask me. If you disagree with her, take it to her."* Our practitioner judgement is that this single act moves more behaviour than a quarter of workshops — offered as judgement, not as measured finding (§14), and testable inside the pilots via the decision-latency proxy.

### 4.3 Sponsorship: a default with a visible opt-out

**Default:** regional sponsors are selected on observed practice — leaders whose own teams already exhibit the four entitlements — rather than on rank.

We acknowledged in v1.0 that this backfires in several regions, then handed the choice back, which was no recommendation at all. The corrected position: the default stands, and a region wishing to depart from it does so through a **one-page note countersigned by the Regional MD and the programme director**, logged in the same register as §3.6. Departures are expected and unremarkable; what matters is that they are visible.

Where the practitioner sponsor sits two or three levels below the Regional MD, the workable form is almost always a **pair** — the senior figure as visible patron providing cover and air, the practitioner as the working engine. A junior sponsor without a senior patron will in several regions be read, reasonably, as the centre not taking the region seriously.

---

## 5. Using the regional cards well

### 5.1 What they are
Starting hypotheses about context, to be returned marked up within 45 days. They describe patterns we have observed in workplaces, not peoples.

### 5.2 What each card contains
Working hypothesis on the four axes · where the gap likely sits · behaviour to add · behaviour to drop · failure mode · **leading indicator observable by day 60** · legal or structural watch item.

### 5.3 The 60-day indicator, and why it is on every card
The failure modes that matter most — courteous non-adoption, affirmative response with no movement — are precisely the ones you cannot detect by asking. Each card therefore names an observable proxy visible within 60 days.

### 5.4 The supersession rule
**Where unit-level diagnostic data exists, it supersedes the card, and the card is retired for that unit.** Within-country variance in work values routinely exceeds between-country variance; function, site history and acquisition lineage frequently dominate nationality. This applies to every card, not only where we have noted it.

### 5.5 Scope note
Cards cover the fourteen clusters where we have wholly-owned or majority-controlled operations. Russia and Belarus are **out of scope** for this programme pending the Group's standing position on those entities; the programme director should not open a workstream there without a written instruction from the sponsor group.

---

## 6. Regional cards

### Card A — Anglosphere (US, Canada, UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand)

| | |
|---|---|
| Working hypothesis | Low authority distance; direct disagreement acceptable; individual error attribution; moderate-to-high ambiguity tolerance |
| Likely gap | Not permission — **follow-through**. Voice is already loud; evidence that it changes anything is thin |
| Add | Visible closure loops: "here is what we did with what you told us, here is what we declined, and why" |
| Drop | Announcing empowerment. The region has heard it and discounts it |
| Failure mode | Ironic compliance; strong survey movement, unchanged decision latency |
| 60-day indicator | Ratio of raised items with a documented, dated response — target 80%+; skip-level uptake |

**Version 1.0 — first circulation. Prepared for sponsor group discussion, and for prior circulation to the delivery leads of the eleven affected programmes and to the four regional engineering directors. Not yet for team-wide communication.**

**Reduce the need for synchronous coordination rather than increasing its supply; fix a thin global core of five team entitlements stated as floors; devolve all norms, rituals, tooling choices and cadence to the teams themselves via a charter they write; run four instrumented pilots with deliberately different designs and identical measurement; and bind the centre and the co-located majority to the same discipline asked of everyone else.**

| Global mandate | **Five entitlements only** (§3) — a named owner for every cross-site dependency; a maximum time-to-first-substantive-response; a discoverable written record of every decision; a route to contribute in writing and, where needed, in one's own language; a stated fallback when work meets a sleeping time zone. Each a floor, each with an alternative-form route (§3.7) |
| Devolved to teams | Channels, tools, ceremony, meeting cadence, standup format, working hours, escalation style, documentation depth, and the team's own vocabulary. Written by the team into a charter (§7) the team owns |
| Structural move | **Time-zone-native ownership** of whole decision classes rather than split ownership across zones (§5.3). This is the intervention we expect to matter most and it is not a communication intervention at all |
| Fairness rule | Out-of-hours meeting burden is **measured, published and rotated**. The co-located majority takes its share (§5.5, §11.2) |
| The centre's obligation | **Corridor decisions are void** until written (§11.1). Reversals of team-level decisions require written reasons to the same audience that saw the decision, counted and reported quarterly |
| Conflict doctrine | Four species distinguished (§8); latency assumed before intent; blameless misunderstanding review; a **bridge role that is earned, rotating and explicitly not managerial** (§8.4) |
| Measurement | Behavioural proxies weighted 70%, survey items 30%; response-style correction applied before any cross-site comparison is shown (§10.2) |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

*Distributed teams do not fail because people are far apart. They fail because work is arranged as though they were not.*

This is our considered practitioner assertion, not a finding — see the evidence key at §15. We flag it because the sponsor group is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are judgement.

The specific failure we are trying to avoid is familiar: a communication programme is launched, a set of norms is published, everyone becomes fluent in the vocabulary of "over-communication" and "assume positive intent," and nothing measurable moves except the survey. That outcome is worse than no initiative, because it consumes the credibility a second attempt would need.

---

## 2. Diagnosis before design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the sponsor group to test

Six candidate drivers produce the same reported symptom. Only two of them respond to communication practice work; two are made *worse* by it.

| Candidate driver | What communication training does to it |
|---|---|
| Too many cross-zone dependencies per unit of work | Nothing — requires work decomposition and ownership redesign (§5) |
| Decision rights held at a site that does not hold the information | **Amplifies harm** — faster, more confident, still wrong |
| Informal context accrues only to the co-located subgroup | Nothing until corridor decisions are made visible and costly (§11.1) |
| No shared written record; decisions live in memory and DMs | Improves, *if* paired with funded documentation time (§3.4) |
| Working-language asymmetry suppresses contribution | Nothing — needs channel design and drafting time, not confidence-building (§6.4) |
| Genuine norm divergence on directness, deadlines, escalation | **Improves** — this is the part the initiative is actually good at (§4) |
| Unanswered questions carry no consequence for anyone | **Worsens** — a further unanswered invitation deepens cynicism |

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Five weeks. No design freeze until it reports.

| Component | Detail |
|---|---|
| Dependency map | For six representative project teams: every cross-site dependency, its owner, its median wait. This is the single most informative artefact and we have never once found it already to exist |
| Latency instrumentation | Retrospective pull from existing ticketing and repository systems: time-to-first-substantive-response, by site pair, by direction. **Aggregate only; §12** |
| Silence audit | Threads and requests that received no substantive response at all within 10 working days. Counted, not attributed |
| Structured conversations | 48 conversations across four levels in seven countries, including at least two teams whose members have never met |

Framed as what a team member is *entitled to*, not as how anyone must behave — so that very different conduct can honour the same floor.

### 3.1 Entitlement I — every cross-site dependency has a named owner
**Floor:** any member can name, for each thing their work waits on, a single named person and the decision that is awaited. Not a team, not a distribution list, not a role — a person. Where nobody can be named, the dependency is escalated as a *design* defect, not a behavioural one.

### 3.2 Entitlement II — there is a maximum time-to-first-substantive-response, and it is visible
**Floor:** each team publishes latency classes and holds to them.

| Class | Response commitment (default, teams may set their own) |
|---|---|
| Blocking — work stopped | One working day of the recipient, with a named fallback if unavailable |
| Consequential, not blocking | Two working days |
| Everything else | Best effort, explicitly no commitment |

*"I have read this, I cannot answer until Thursday, here is who can"* satisfies the floor. Silence does not. **The floor is the acknowledgement, not the answer** — this distinction is the whole of it, and teams that miss it produce anxiety rather than speed.

### 3.3 Entitlement III — decisions are discoverable in writing
**Floor:** any decision that changes what someone else must do exists, within 24 hours, in a location a new joiner could find unaided. Format devolved entirely — a paragraph in a channel is sufficient. Length is not the point; findability is.

### 3.4 Entitlement IV — there is a written route in, and language is not a tax on contribution
**Floor:** every member has at least one channel through which they may contribute, and disagree, **in writing and asynchronously**, and receive a response. It need never be a spoken objection on a live call in a second language.

Where a member's working-language fluency is materially below the team median, they are entitled to draft in their own language with machine translation, and to have that carry the same weight. This is a floor because the alternative — treating fluency as a proxy for contribution — is both unjust and expensively wrong.

### 3.5 Entitlement V — no work sleeps without a stated fallback
**Floor:** for each work item crossing a time-zone boundary, either a named person in the receiving zone can progress it, or the handover states explicitly that it will wait and until when. **The prohibited state is not delay. It is undeclared delay.**

### 3.6 Everything else is the team's property
Tools, cadence, standups, ceremony, documentation depth, escalation style, core hours, camera norms, emoji conventions, and the team's own name for all of this. We would suggest the centre resist standardising even the vocabulary.

### 3.7 The alternative-form process (in place of exemption)

We avoid the word *exemption*, and avoid asking any team to refuse. A team that cannot meet a floor is asked instead to **propose the nearest form it can honour**, and to state the condition under which the floor becomes reachable.

| Element | Provision |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Legal impossibility, collective-agreement conflict, client-contractual conflict, or structural impossibility — not difficulty, not preference |
| Form | Two pages: which floor, why, the alternative mechanism, the condition that would close the gap |
| Approver | Programme director, countersigned by the regional engineering director and, where data or monitoring is implicated, Group Legal |
| Duration | 12 months, renewable once with fresh reasoning |
| Visibility | Internally published register, reviewed quarterly |
| Presumption | Accepted unless materially weaker than the floor. We expect three to six across the network in Year 1 and would be suspicious of zero |

---

## 4. The adaptation logic

### 4.1 Four axes, not a culture model

We would ask each team to place *itself* — not its nationalities — on four axes, because these four determine whether a given practice functions or backfires.

| Axis | The question | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Directness of disagreement** | Can dissent be public without cost to either party? | Whether the dissent route can be a live call, or must be written and private (Entitlement IV) |
| **Context density** | Is meaning carried in the words, or in what surrounds them? | How much explicit writing is required before a message is complete |
| **Authority basis** | Does authority derive from role, or from demonstrated expertise? | Whether devolved ownership reads as trust or as abandonment |
| **Time orientation** | Is a date a commitment, a forecast, or an aspiration? | Whether "on track" means the same thing on both ends of a call |

### 4.2 The working rule

> Low disagreement-directness does not mean people have nothing to say. It means **the channel is wrong, not the culture**. An open invitation on a live call in a second language in front of a senior colleague is not an invitation; it is a test most people will sensibly decline to sit.

The functioning equivalent is almost always: written, asynchronous, addressed to a named person, with time to draft, and — where face matters — routed so that no one is corrected in public. Our practitioner judgement is that moving the dissent channel from spoken-live to written-async recovers more suppressed information than any amount of psychological-safety framing. Offered as judgement (§15), and testable inside the pilots via the silence audit.

### 4.3 The four misreadings we expect

| One side does | The other reads | The actual meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Answers "yes, we can look at that" | Commitment | Acknowledgement of the request's legitimacy |
| Sends a three-line message with no preamble | Coldness, possible anger | Efficiency, and respect for the reader's time |
| Reports "on track" until the week before | Concealment | Reluctance to escalate upward without a solution in hand |
| Goes silent for two days | Disengagement | A public holiday nobody outside that country had heard of |

The last one is not a joke. A shared holiday-and-absence calendar, visible by default, retires a meaningful share of reported "misunderstandings" for approximately no money. We would put it in the first thirty days.

---

## 5. Time-zone architecture — the part that is not about communication

### 5.1 The arithmetic, stated plainly

| Overlap between two sites | What is realistically possible |
|---|---|
| 4+ hours | Genuinely collaborative work; joint problem-solving |
| 2–3 hours | Coordination and decision-making; not sustained joint work |
| 0–1 hours | **Handover only.** Any design that assumes more will fail, and no amount of goodwill will rescue it |

### 5.2 The default we recommend

Redraw team boundaries so that each **decision loop** sits inside a zone band with ≥4 hours of overlap, and each **handover** sits at a band boundary that is documented and deliberately chosen. Cross-band dependency count becomes a tracked engineering metric with a target, in the same manner as build time.

### 5.3 Time-zone-native ownership

Where possible, give a whole decision class to the region that holds the working hours for it, rather than splitting it and coordinating. This trades some consistency for a large reduction in latency. We regard the trade as clearly worth making and would rather argue it openly than smuggle it in.

### 5.4 Three experiments we would like permission to run

The persona of this programme is exploratory by design; these are cheap, reversible and instrumented.

| Experiment | Duration | What it tests |
|---|---|---|
| **Async-only fortnight** — all recurring cross-zone meetings cancelled, nothing else changed | 2 weeks, two pilot teams | How much of our meeting load is coordination and how much is habit. We expect to be surprised in both directions |
| **Reverse-hours quarter** — the largest co-located site takes the unsociable slot for all cross-zone calls | 1 quarter, one pilot | Whether the burden is tolerable when it is reciprocal, and what the co-located site learns from carrying it |
| **Bounty board** — unblocked dependencies published openly; any qualified person in any zone may claim and resolve one | 1 quarter | Whether latency is caused by capacity or by ownership routing |

# Critique — "Distributed Team Effectiveness Initiative, v1.0"

## Verdict in one line

There is a genuinely good paper buried in here — the dependency-architecture reframe, the written-async dissent insight and the overlap arithmetic are the best thinking in either document — but what has been delivered is roughly 40% of a deliverable, it silently drops one of the three things the brief explicitly asked for, and it imports a governance template from an unrelated programme without testing whether it fits.

---

## 1. Critical defects

### 1.1 The document stops mid-sentence at §5.5
Sections 6 through 15 do not exist. They are not deferred, they are referenced — I count **31 forward references** to material that was never written: the team charter (§7), the conflict doctrine (§8), the team cards (§9), measurement (§10), the centre's obligations (§11), the data and consultation gates (§12), the budget assumptions (§14), the evidence key (§15). The reader is told twice that §15 will tell them which claims are evidenced and which are judgement; §15 does not exist, so the paper's central honesty device is a promissory note that is never redeemed. This is not a formatting issue. A sponsor group cannot act on it.

### 1.2 Conflict resolution — one-third of the brief — is absent
The request asked for three things: communication, collaboration, and **conflict resolution**. Conflict appears once, as a summary-table teaser ("four species distinguished (§8)... a bridge role that is earned, rotating and explicitly not managerial"). The teaser is intriguing and entirely unbacked. Nothing in the delivered text addresses:

- an escalation ladder with timeboxes and named arbiters;
- who mediates when the parties sit in different reporting lines, different legal entities and different countries;
- the distinction between task, process, relationship and status conflict, and why the remedy differs for each;
- the specific distributed pathology that **text escalates and voice de-escalates** — a rule that conflict which has survived two written exchanges moves to a call, with a neutral third present, is worth more than most of §3;
- the cross-cultural face problem, where the injury *is* the public correction, and the remedy is routing rather than reframing;
- the rule that no conflict is resolved in a channel where only one party's colleagues are watching.

### 1.3 Template transfer without a fit test
The structural inheritance from the prior employee-empowerment paper is close to total: "How we would ask you to use this," "one note, then the substance," "recommendation on a page," entitlements-as-floors, the alternative-form process "in place of exemption," the 60%/30%/nil offset, "we would be suspicious of zero," "the line most often cut and most often fatal," "the cheapest consequential decision," "worse than no initiative, because it consumes the credibility a second attempt would need," "cards returned unamended will be read not as agreement."

Two problems. First, if both papers reach the same sponsor group — and they plainly will — the second one reads as a mail-merge of the first, and every sentence of hard-won judgement in it gets discounted. Second, the template is genuinely wrong in places for this problem. A team-level delivery friction does not obviously warrant a two-page filing countersigned by a regional engineering director in order to vary a response-time norm. The empowerment programme needed that machinery because it was touching statutory entitlements. This one mostly isn't.

### 1.4 Register mismatch: nothing ships for five months
Teams are missing dates *today*. The paper offers a five-week diagnostic, a design phase, a sponsor decision on 22 April, then pilots. Meanwhile it identifies, almost in passing at §4.3, that a shared holiday-and-absence calendar "retires a meaningful share of reported misunderstandings for approximately no money" — and then buries it in a footnote-grade aside.

**There must be a no-regrets track running in parallel with the diagnostic**, comprising interventions that cannot be wrong regardless of what the diagnostic finds: the holiday calendar; published per-person working hours and overlap windows on every team page; a single decision log per team; response-class norms; a rule that if one participant is remote, everyone joins individually. Days, not months, and near-zero cost. Its absence makes the paper look like a consultancy protecting its diagnostic phase.

---

## 2. Substantive weaknesses in what *was* written

### 2.1 The primary metric is trivially gameable, and the paper builds the exploit itself
§3.2 states, correctly and well, that *"the floor is the acknowledgement, not the answer."* §1 then makes **median time-to-first-substantive-response** the headline behavioural proxy and the arm of the failure test. So the programme's core metric is satisfied by a two-line "got it, Thursday." Within a quarter you will have excellent latency numbers and identical blocked-work hours.

Fix: pair every latency metric with a counter-metric that cannot move in the same direction for free — time-to-*resolution* on blocking items, reopened-thread rate, or proportion of acknowledgements that are followed by the promised substantive reply within the stated date. Say explicitly which metric wins when they conflict.

### 2.2 Who classifies a request as "blocking"?
The three-tier latency table never says. Sender-classification produces universal inflation within six weeks — everything becomes blocking. Recipient-classification produces deflation and defeats the entitlement. This is the standard failure mode of every SLA scheme ever deployed and the paper walks past it. The workable answer is sender-classifies, recipient may reclassify with a reason, disputes go to the dependency owner, and misclassification rates are visible per person — but *some* answer is required.

### 2.3 There is no consequence for breaching a floor
§2.1 diagnoses, sharply, that "unanswered questions carry no consequence for anyone." The five entitlements then create no consequence for anyone. The alternative-form register handles *declared* non-compliance; nothing handles quiet non-compliance, which is the actual behaviour. What happens on the third breach, and who sees it?

### 2.4 Entitlement I creates the single point of failure it is trying to remove
"A single named person. Not a team, not a distribution list, not a role." Directionally right, operationally brittle: that person takes leave, changes team, or leaves the company. It also collides with Entitlement V, which requires a fallback. Needs named owner **plus** named deputy, an explicit reassignment rule, and — the harder point — an acknowledgement that in a matrixed organisation the named owner frequently has no authority over the resource. Naming without authority is accountability theatre and will be recognised as such.

### 2.5 Entitlement III is internally contradictory
The floor is *findability by a new joiner unaided*. §3.6 then devolves tooling entirely to teams. Across eleven programmes with free tool choice, cross-team findability is arithmetically impossible; you will have eleven decision logs in six systems with no common schema. Either findability is a global floor or storage is fully local — not both. Recommend a deliberately thin interoperability standard (one search surface, a five-field decision-record schema, a common item identifier) with everything else left free. That is a small concession that rescues the entitlement.

### 2.6 The machine-translation entitlement is under-engineered and has an unflagged legal problem
The instinct is right and humane. But: routing internal technical discussion through public translation engines is a data-transfer and confidentiality issue, and the paper names a Data Protection Officer without noticing this. Also required — a domain glossary (MT mangles precisely the technical and contractual terms that matter), a rule on which text is the *record*, and a check on whether the translated contribution actually carries equal weight in practice rather than in policy.

### 2.7 §5 is the best section and elides its own hard part
"Redraw team boundaries" and "give a whole decision class to the region that holds the working hours" are the right recommendations. §5.3 characterises the trade as "some consistency for a large reduction in latency." That understates it considerably. The real costs are duplicated capability, standards divergence, key-person concentration in a single geography, narrowed career paths for people outside the owning zone, and — in several jurisdictions — a works council consultation obligation for moving work between countries. The paper flags consultation for *monitoring* and misses it for *restructuring*, which is by far the larger exposure. Say this openly; the section's credibility rests on it.

Also missing: the relay/follow-the-sun option (A→B→C partial-overlap chains), which is the standard alternative to the "one owning zone" answer and deserves at least a paragraph on why it is or isn't preferred here.

### 2.8 The overlap table is presented as arithmetic and is actually judgement
4+ / 2–3 / 0–1 hours with hard verdicts attached. These are reasonable practitioner thresholds; they are not arithmetic, and the paper has just made a virtue of tagging its judgements. Tag this one. Also note that overlap can be manufactured through shifted or split hours — at a human cost that should be named rather than assumed away.

### 2.9 The experiments are good and two of them are unsafe as drafted
- **Reverse-hours quarter**: three months of unsociable hours imposed on the largest site is a wellbeing matter, a working-time-regulation matter in the EU, and in several jurisdictions a consultation matter. It needs individual opt-out, a health check-in, a shorter first tranche, and the same §12 gate the paper insists on for measurement.
- **Bounty board**: needs guardrails on access control, code review quality, cherry-picking of easy items, and unfunded discretionary effort. As drafted it also quietly contradicts Entitlement I's named-owner rule.
- **Async-only fortnight**: two weeks is too short. Week one runs on residual context and looks fine; the breakage appears in week three. Run it for two full delivery cycles or six weeks.

### 2.10 A sequencing contradiction in the paper's own governance
The opening insists that §12 clear with Legal, the DPO and the EWC **"before any measurement is switched on."** §2.2 then proposes, as the first activity, a retrospective pull from ticketing and repository systems, calendar metadata and a thread-level silence audit. That is measurement.
[END QUALITY FEEDBACK]

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

*Distributed teams do not fail because people are far apart. They fail because work is arranged as though they were not.*

This is our considered practitioner assertion, not a finding — see the evidence key at §15. We flag it because the sponsor group is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are judgement.

The specific failure we are trying to avoid is familiar: a communication programme is launched, a set of norms is published, everyone becomes fluent in the vocabulary of "over-communication" and "assume positive intent," and nothing measurable moves except the survey. That outcome is worse than no initiative, because it consumes the credibility a second attempt would need.

## 2. Diagnosis before design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the sponsor group to test

Six candidate drivers produce the same reported symptom. Only two of them respond to communication practice work; two are made *worse* by it.

| Candidate driver | What communication training does to it |
|---|---|
| Too many cross-zone dependencies per unit of work | Nothing — requires work decomposition and ownership redesign (§5) |
| Decision rights held at a site that does not hold the information | **Amplifies harm** — faster, more confident, still wrong |
| Informal context accrues only to the co-located subgroup | Nothing until corridor decisions are made visible and costly (§11.1) |
| No shared written record; decisions live in memory and DMs | Improves, *if* paired with funded documentation time (§3.4) |
| Working-language asymmetry suppresses contribution | Nothing — needs channel design and drafting time, not confidence-building (§6.4) |
| Genuine norm divergence on directness, deadlines, escalation | **Improves** — this is the part the initiative is actually good at (§4) |
| Unanswered questions carry no consequence for anyone | **Worsens** — a further unanswered invitation deepens cynicism |

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Five weeks. No design freeze until it reports.

| Component | Detail |
|---|---|
| Dependency map | For six representative project teams: every cross-site dependency, its owner, its median wait. This is the single most informative artefact and we have never once found it already to exist |
| Latency instrumentation | Retrospective pull from existing ticketing and repository systems: time-to-first-substantive-response, by site pair, by direction. **Aggregate only; §12** |
| Silence audit | Threads and requests that received no substantive response at all within 10 working days. Counted, not attributed |
| Structured conversations | 48 conversations across four levels in seven countries, including at least two teams whose members have never met |
| Meeting burden ledger | Out-of-hours synchronous hours per person per site, from calendar metadata, aggregated by site |
| Language check | The four teams whose working language is not the local language of the majority of members |
| Cost | **$185K** |

**The decision this buys.** If the dependency map shows high cross-zone dependency density, the Year 1 budget should move substantially from practice-and-behaviour work into work decomposition and ownership redesign, and the pilot scope should be rewritten before commitment. This is the cheapest consequential decision available to us, and we would rather make it in May than discover it in November.

## 3. What is fixed everywhere: five entitlements, stated as floors

Framed as what a team member is *entitled to*, not as how anyone must behave — so that very different conduct can honour the same floor.

### 3.1 Entitlement I — every cross-site dependency has a named owner
**Floor:** any member can name, for each thing their work waits on, a single named person and the decision that is awaited. Not a team, not a distribution list, not a role — a person. Where nobody can be named, the dependency is escalated as a *design* defect, not a behavioural one.

### 3.2 Entitlement II — there is a maximum time-to-first-substantive-response, and it is visible
**Floor:** each team publishes latency classes and holds to them.

| Class | Response commitment (default, teams may set their own) |
|---|---|
| Blocking — work stopped | One working day of the recipient, with a named fallback if unavailable |
| Consequential, not blocking | Two working days |
| Everything else | Best effort, explicitly no commitment |

*"I have read this, I cannot answer until Thursday, here is who can"* satisfies the floor. Silence does not. **The floor is the acknowledgement, not the answer** — this distinction is the whole of it, and teams that miss it produce anxiety rather than speed.

### 3.3 Entitlement III — decisions are discoverable in writing
**Floor:** any decision that changes what someone else must do exists, within 24 hours, in a location a new joiner could find unaided. Format devolved entirely — a paragraph in a channel is sufficient. Length is not the point; findability is.

### 3.4 Entitlement IV — there is a written route in, and language is not a tax on contribution
**Floor:** every member has at least one channel through which they may contribute, and disagree, **in writing and asynchronously**, and receive a response. It need never be a spoken objection on a live call in a second language.

Where a member's working-language fluency is materially below the team median, they are entitled to draft in their own language with machine translation, and to have that carry the same weight. This is a floor because the alternative — treating fluency as a proxy for contribution — is both unjust and expensively wrong.

### 3.5 Entitlement V — no work sleeps without a stated fallback
**Floor:** for each work item crossing a time-zone boundary, either a named person in the receiving zone can progress it, or the handover states explicitly that it will wait and until when. **The prohibited state is not delay. It is undeclared delay.**

### 3.6 Everything else is the team's property
Tools, cadence, standups, ceremony, documentation depth, escalation style, core hours, camera norms, emoji conventions, and the team's own name for all of this. We would suggest the centre resist standardising even the vocabulary.

### 3.7 The alternative-form process (in place of exemption)

We avoid the word *exemption*, and avoid asking any team to refuse. A team that cannot meet a floor is asked instead to **propose the nearest form it can honour**, and to state the condition under which the floor becomes reachable.

| Element | Provision |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Legal impossibility, collective-agreement conflict, client-contractual conflict, or structural impossibility — not difficulty, not preference |
| Form | Two pages: which floor, why, the alternative mechanism, the condition that would close the gap |
| Approver | Programme director, countersigned by the regional engineering director and, where data or monitoring is implicated, Group Legal |
| Duration | 12 months, renewable once with fresh reasoning |
| Visibility | Internally published register, reviewed quarterly |
| Presumption | Accepted unless materially weaker than the floor. We expect three to six across the network in Year 1 and would be suspicious of zero |

## 4. The adaptation logic

### 4.1 Four axes, not a culture model

We would ask each team to place *itself* — not its nationalities — on four axes, because these four determine whether a given practice functions or backfires.

| Axis | The question | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Directness of disagreement** | Can dissent be public without cost to either party? | Whether the dissent route can be a live call, or must be written and private (Entitlement IV) |
| **Context density** | Is meaning carried in the words, or in what surrounds them? | How much explicit writing is required before a message is complete |
| **Authority basis** | Does authority derive from role, or from demonstrated expertise? | Whether devolved ownership reads as trust or as abandonment |
| **Time orientation** | Is a date a commitment, a forecast, or an aspiration? | Whether "on track" means the same thing on both ends of a call |

### 4.2 The working rule

> Low disagreement-directness does not mean people have nothing to say. It means **the channel is wrong, not the culture**. An open invitation on a live call in a second language in front of a senior colleague is not an invitation; it is a test most people will sensibly decline to sit.

The functioning equivalent is almost always: written, asynchronous, addressed to a named person, with time to draft, and — where face matters — routed so that no one is corrected in public. Our practitioner judgement is that moving the dissent channel from spoken-live to written-async recovers more suppressed information than any amount of psychological-safety framing. Offered as judgement (§15), and testable inside the pilots via the silence audit.

### 4.3 The four misreadings we expect

| One side does | The other reads | The actual meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Answers "yes, we can look at that" | Commitment | Acknowledgement of the request's legitimacy |
| Sends a three-line message with no preamble | Coldness, possible anger | Efficiency, and respect for the reader's time |
| Reports "on track" until the week before | Concealment | Reluctance to escalate upward without a solution in hand |
| Goes silent for two days | Disengagement | A public holiday nobody outside that country had heard of |

The last one is not a joke. A shared holiday-and-absence calendar, visible by default, retires a meaningful share of reported "misunderstandings" for approximately no money. We would put it in the first thirty days.

## 5. Time-zone architecture — the part that is not about communication

### 5.1 The arithmetic, stated plainly

| Overlap between two sites | What is realistically possible |
|---|---|
| 4+ hours | Genuinely collaborative work; joint problem-solving |
| 2–3 hours | Coordination and decision-making; not sustained joint work |
| 0–1 hours | **Handover only.** Any design that assumes more will fail, and no amount of goodwill will rescue it |

### 5.2 The default we recommend

Redraw team boundaries so that each **decision loop** sits inside a zone band with ≥4 hours of overlap, and each **handover** sits at a band boundary that is documented and deliberately chosen. Cross-band dependency count becomes a tracked engineering metric with a target, in the same manner as build time.

### 5.3 Time-zone-native ownership

Where possible, give a whole decision class to the region that holds the working hours for it, rather than splitting it and coordinating. This trades some consistency for a large reduction in latency. We regard the trade as clearly worth making and would rather argue it openly than smuggle it in.

### 5.4 Three experiments we would like permission to run

The persona of this programme is exploratory by design; these are cheap, reversible and instrumented.

| Experiment | Duration | What it tests |
|---|---|---|
| **Async-only fortnight** — all recurring cross-zone meetings cancelled, nothing else changed | 2 weeks, two pilot teams | How much of our meeting load is coordination and how much is habit. We expect to be surprised in both directions |
| **Reverse-hours quarter** — the largest co-located site takes the unsociable slot for all cross-zone calls | 1 quarter, one pilot | Whether the burden is tolerable when it is reciprocal, and what the co-located site learns from carrying it |
| **Bounty board** — unblocked dependencies published openly; any qualified person in any zone may claim and resolve one | 1 quarter | Whether latency is caused by capacity or by ownership routing |

# Critique — "Distributed Team Effectiveness Initiative, v1.0"

## Verdict in one line

There is a genuinely good paper buried in here — the dependency-architecture reframe, the written-async dissent insight and the overlap arithmetic are the best thinking in either document — but what has been delivered is roughly 40% of a deliverable, it silently drops one of the three things the brief explicitly asked for, and it imports a governance template from an unrelated programme without testing whether it fits.

---

## 1. Critical defects

### 1.1 The document stops mid-sentence at §5.5
Sections 6 through 15 do not exist. They are not deferred, they are referenced — I count **31 forward references** to material that was never written: the team charter (§7), the conflict doctrine (§8), the team cards (§9), measurement (§10), the centre's obligations (§11), the data and consultation gates (§12), the budget assumptions (§14), the evidence key (§15). The reader is told twice that §15 will tell them which claims are evidenced and which are judgement; §15 does not exist, so the paper's central honesty device is a promissory note that is never redeemed. This is not a formatting issue. A sponsor group cannot act on it.

### 1.2 Conflict resolution — one-third of the brief — is absent
The request asked for three things: communication, collaboration, and **conflict resolution**. Conflict appears once, as a summary-table teaser ("four species distinguished (§8)... a bridge role that is earned, rotating and explicitly not managerial"). The teaser is intriguing and entirely unbacked. Nothing in the delivered text addresses:

- an escalation ladder with timeboxes and named arbiters;
- who mediates when the parties sit in different reporting lines, different legal entities and different countries;
- the distinction between task, process, relationship and status conflict, and why the remedy differs for each;
- the specific distributed pathology that **text escalates and voice de-escalates** — a rule that conflict which has survived two written exchanges moves to a call, with a neutral third present, is worth more than most of §3;
- the cross-cultural face problem, where the injury *is* the public correction, and the remedy is routing rather than reframing;
- the rule that no conflict is resolved in a channel where only one party's colleagues are watching.

### 1.3 Template transfer without a fit test
The structural inheritance from the prior employee-empowerment paper is close to total: "How we would ask you to use this," "one note, then the substance," "recommendation on a page," entitlements-as-floors, the alternative-form process "in place of exemption," the 60%/30%/nil offset, "we would be suspicious of zero," "the line most often cut and most often fatal," "the cheapest consequential decision," "worse than no initiative, because it consumes the credibility a second attempt would need," "cards returned unamended will be read not as agreement."

Two problems. First, if both papers reach the same sponsor group — and they plainly will — the second one reads as a mail-merge of the first, and every sentence of hard-won judgement in it gets discounted. Second, the template is genuinely wrong in places for this problem. A team-level delivery friction does not obviously warrant a two-page filing countersigned by a regional engineering director in order to vary a response-time norm. The empowerment programme needed that machinery because it was touching statutory entitlements. This one mostly isn't.

### 1.4 Register mismatch: nothing ships for five months
Teams are missing dates *today*. The paper offers a five-week diagnostic, a design phase, a sponsor decision on 22 April, then pilots. Meanwhile it identifies, almost in passing at §4.3, that a shared holiday-and-absence calendar "retires a meaningful share of reported misunderstandings for approximately no money" — and then buries it in a footnote-grade aside.

**There must be a no-regrets track running in parallel with the diagnostic**, comprising interventions that cannot be wrong regardless of what the diagnostic finds: the holiday calendar; published per-person working hours and overlap windows on every team page; a single decision log per team; response-class norms; a rule that if one participant is remote, everyone joins individually. Days, not months, and near-zero cost. Its absence makes the paper look like a consultancy protecting its diagnostic phase.

## 2. Substantive weaknesses in what *was* written

### 2.1 The primary metric is trivially gameable, and the paper builds the exploit itself
§3.2 states, correctly and well, that *"the floor is the acknowledgement, not the answer."* §1 then makes **median time-to-first-substantive-response** the headline behavioural proxy and the arm of the failure test. So the programme's core metric is satisfied by a two-line "got it, Thursday." Within a quarter you will have excellent latency numbers and identical blocked-work hours.

Fix: pair every latency metric with a counter-metric that cannot move in the same direction for free — time-to-*resolution* on blocking items, reopened-thread rate, or proportion of acknowledgements that are followed by the promised substantive reply within the stated date. Say explicitly which metric wins when they conflict.

### 2.2 Who classifies a request as "blocking"?
The three-tier latency table never says. Sender-classification produces universal inflation within six weeks — everything becomes blocking. Recipient-classification produces deflation and defeats the entitlement. This is the standard failure mode of every SLA scheme ever deployed and the paper walks past it. The workable answer is sender-classifies, recipient may reclassify with a reason, disputes go to the dependency owner, and misclassification rates are visible per person — but *some* answer is required.

### 2.3 There is no consequence for breaching a floor
§2.1 diagnoses, sharply, that "unanswered questions carry no consequence for anyone." The five entitlements then create no consequence for anyone. The alternative-form register handles *declared* non-compliance; nothing handles quiet non-compliance, which is the actual behaviour. What happens on the third breach, and who sees it?

### 2.4 Entitlement I creates the single point of failure it is trying to remove
"A single named person. Not a team, not a distribution list, not a role." Directionally right, operationally brittle: that person takes leave, changes team, or leaves the company. It also collides with Entitlement V, which requires a fallback. Needs named owner **plus** named deputy, an explicit reassignment rule, and — the harder point — an acknowledgement that in a matrixed organisation the named owner frequently has no authority over the resource. Naming without authority is accountability theatre and will be recognised as such.

### 2.5 Entitlement III is internally contradictory
The floor is *findability by a new joiner unaided*. §3.6 then devolves tooling entirely to teams. Across eleven programmes with free tool choice, cross-team findability is arithmetically impossible; you will have eleven decision logs in six systems with no common schema. Either findability is a global floor or storage is fully local — not both. Recommend a deliberately thin interoperability standard (one search surface, a five-field decision-record schema, a common item identifier) with everything else left free. That is a small concession that rescues the entitlement.

### 2.6 The machine-translation entitlement is under-engineered and has an unflagged legal problem
The instinct is right and humane. But: routing internal technical discussion through public translation engines is a data-transfer and confidentiality issue, and the paper names a Data Protection Officer without noticing this. Also required — a domain glossary (MT mangles precisely the technical and contractual terms that matter), a rule on which text is the *record*, and a check on whether the translated contribution actually carries equal weight in practice rather than in policy.

### 2.7 §5 is the best section and elides its own hard part
"Redraw team boundaries" and "give a whole decision class to the region that holds the working hours" are the right recommendations. §5.3 characterises the trade as "some consistency for a large reduction in latency." That understates it considerably. The real costs are duplicated capability, standards divergence, key-person concentration in a single geography, narrowed career paths for people outside the owning zone, and — in several jurisdictions — a works council consultation obligation for moving work between countries. The paper flags consultation for *monitoring* and misses it for *restructuring*, which is by far the larger exposure. Say this openly; the section's credibility rests on it.

Also missing: the relay/follow-the-sun option (A→B→C partial-overlap chains), which is the standard alternative to the "one owning zone" answer and deserves at least a paragraph on why it is or isn't preferred here.

### 2.8 The overlap table is presented as arithmetic and is actually judgement
4+ / 2–3 / 0–1 hours with hard verdicts attached. These are reasonable practitioner thresholds; they are not arithmetic, and the paper has just made a virtue of tagging its judgements. Tag this one. Also note that overlap can be manufactured through shifted or split hours — at a human cost that should be named rather than assumed away.

### 2.9 The experiments are good and two of them are unsafe as drafted
- **Reverse-hours quarter**: three months of unsociable hours imposed on the largest site is a wellbeing matter, a working-time-regulation matter in the EU, and in several jurisdictions a consultation matter. It needs individual opt-out, a health check-in, a shorter first tranche, and the same §12 gate the paper insists on for measurement.
- **Bounty board**: needs guardrails on access control, code review quality, cherry-picking of easy items, and unfunded discretionary effort. As drafted it also quietly contradicts Entitlement I's named-owner rule.
- **Async-only fortnight**: two weeks is too short. Week one runs on residual context and looks fine; the breakage appears in week three. Run it for two full delivery cycles or six weeks.

### 2.10 A sequencing contradiction in the paper's own governance
The opening insists that §12 clear with Legal, the DPO and the EWC **"before any measurement is switched on."** §2.2 then proposes, as the first activity, a retrospective pull from ticketing and repository systems, calendar metadata and a thread-level silence audit. That is measurement.
